newsitem.title: USA: Gore predicts TV ratings deal within 24-48 hours.
newsitem.headline: Gore predicts TV ratings deal within 24-48 hours.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore Wednesday predicted a deal within the next day or two between television executives and parents' groups on revamping the industry's programme ratings.

"I think we're on the verge within the next 24 to 48 hours of having a final agreement that will allow them (television executives) some grace period and some time to implement this," Gore told the Cable News Network.

Talks between the two groups at the headquarters of the Motion Picture Association of America in Washington centre on the existing age-based system, which includes TV-14 for parents of children under 14. Parent groups and congressional lawmakers feel the system, introduced at the start of 1997, does not go far enough and is too vague.

"What's going on right now is the fine tuning of that rating system to make sure that for young children, and all children, there is information available to parents with which they can protect their children from material they think may not be appropriate for them," Gore said.

Industry representatives have agreed to add the letters "V," "S" and "L" to their 6-month-old system to designate sexual content, violence and coarse language, a source familiar with the talks said Tuesday. The designations would be added to the TV-PG (parental guidance suggested), TV-14 and TV-M (mature audiences only) ratings.

Television executives faced a Tuesday deadline from members of the Senate who insisted the industry develop a ratings system that satisfies parent groups -- or face legislation that would require changes.

Industry representatives broke off negotiations late last week after Gore urged the industry to include the V, S and L ratings. The National Association of Broadcasters, which is participating in the talks, called Gore's statement at the time "unwarranted intervention."

But Gore sounded upbeat about the latest round of talks. "I think that while there has always been some resistance on the part of a few in the industry, the leaders in the industry have long tried to work this out," he told CNN.
